title: Pain regulation through interaction of mood and expectation within and across pain modalities
summary:
Many people who suffer from chronic abdominal pain—such as those with irritable bowel syndrome or chronic inflammatory bowel diseases—experience that their pain cannot be sufficiently relieved despite repeated treatments. Psychological factors such as mood and expectations can play an important role in this process but have not been sufficiently studied. In particular, little is known about how a negative mood—such as that occurring in depression—affects the efficacy of pain treatments.

In this study, we investigate in healthy participants how a sad mood, compared to a neutral mood, influences the perception and evaluation of pain during a pharmacological, analgesic treatment. We compare two types of pain: abdominal pain induced by rectal distension (visceral pain), and skin surface pain induced by heat stimuli (somatic pain). A special focus is placed on the influence of expectations and prior treatment experiences on pain responses over the course of treatment. 
To better understand individual differences, we also assess various psychological and biological characteristics of the participants. This enables us to examine learning and memory processes that may play a role in the effects of repeated treatments. 
Our goal is to identify psychobiological mechanisms that explain how psychological factors influence pain perception in the treatment context—particularly for visceral pain. The findings aim to contribute to the development of more personalized and effective therapies for people with chronic pain.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
fluent in German, BMI 18-30
Exclusion criteria:
- Acute and chronic physical illnesses (e.g., pain disorders, gastrointestinal diseases, cardiovascular diseases)
- Regular use of medication (except hormon or thyroid replacement; allergy medications)
- Indications of psychiatric disorders based on validated screening instruments (especially depression and anxiety disorders) and/or self-report
- MRI-specific exclusion criteria (anxiety disorders, especially claustrophobia, metallic implants, metal-containing tattoos, etc.)
- Additional exclusion criterion: Indication of anorectal abnormalities (e.g., hemorrhoids), identified during screening or medical examination (including digital rectal exam) prior to placement of the rectal balloon catheter for pressure-controlled rectal distension as an established visceral pain model
- Additional exclusion criterion for female participants: Pregnancy or breastfeeding
